rv.q: Birch has crafted a rich, haunting, technically dazzling script, in which the women cast eerie shadows through time.
The play is both riveting and static.
Anatomy of a Suicide is a powerful, unflinching look at a family afflicted with severe depression and mental illness.

Alice Birch, darling of the film world after her stark and powerful script for Lady Macbeth, returns in triumph to her home ground of the theatre for an unflinching examination of three generations of women in one family tormented by severe depression and mental illness.
It is an extraordinary echoing text, full of pain and strange beauty.
And yet, finally, such vague misgivings pale beside the essential bravery and daring of it all.
It’s a play that raises many more questions than it answers but for two uninterrupted hours it kept me hooked.
Though it is hard to imagine anyone actually enjoying this show, it will be admired for its assured production.
"Anatomy of a Suicide" is a shimmeringly powerful puzzle play that respects, and rewards, the attention of its audience.
When their house is finally revealed at the end we, the audience feel the light flood in and the weight from Bonnie lifted as she is able to finally put her past to rest.
Sadly, Birch and Mitchell are better at representing darkness than at throwing light on their subject.
It does, in a way, deserve a prize — for the most obtuse script of the year.
Birch has provided a text that explores these ideas in a formally invigorating way.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this formally audacious exploration of inherited trauma across three generations, with most admiring Birch's ambitious structure and Mitchell's meticulous direction, though one finds the experimental approach conceals thin material.
